prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms confined at the magic wavelength are interrogated without light-shift, Doppler or recoil limits, bringing time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B053 to B027, the optical lattice clock credited to Katori and Ye. In round 1 I put spherical-aberration correction first because it fits the test I apply, a discovery or invention with identifiable originators, and I still think it meets that test. But the exchange has changed my judgement in two ways. First, six members from quite different specialities independently reached B027, and their reasons are scientific as much as attributional: the magic-wavelength condition is a concrete idea with a clear before and after, the 10^-18 performance has been reproduced at JILA, Tokyo/RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and the consequences (time-dilation tests at centimetre scale, searches for varying constants and dark matter) are real even if the redefinition of the second is still pending. I do not count that support as a substitute for judgement, but it prompted me to check my own preference against the same test, and B027 meets it at least as cleanly. Second, I am the only member who ranked B053 and I judge it from daily microscopy practice, so the field proximity I disclosed in round 1 is a real reason to discount my own advocacy. A prize that rests on one member's professional enthusiasm is weaker than one whose case survives scrutiny from atomic theorists, an instrument builder and a statistical physicist. The citation should name the optical lattice clock itself and its magic-wavelength principle, so that it separates the achievement from the frequency-comb prize of 2005 and the single-ion prize of 2012.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier precision-measurement prizes is the strongest objection and I do not think it can be fully dismissed. The clock relies on comb and ultrastable-laser technology that Hall and Haensch and others already received recognition for, and on laser cooling and trapping. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept for interrogating many neutral atoms, not a refinement of ion-trap work, and that the citation must say so. I also remain somewhat uneasy that Ye's contribution is partly the pushing of accuracy and stability, rather than a separate concept; I accept the pairing because Katori is the originator of the concept and Ye is the leader of its extreme-performance demonstration and broad use, and the two names together give the least contested allocation on the shortlist. Other costs I accept knowingly: ion-clock pioneers, early Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers are outside the credit, and part of the headline impact is still prospective. Finally, B053 is lost as a candidate this year, and with it an instrument whose originators are traceable; I regard that as a loss for the field I know best, but not a reason to hold the committee back.

responses.point: Kroll treats the lattice clock as a clean instrument-level invention with confirmation by many independent laboratories and a natural two-person credit, and wants the broader community credit handled by narrow framing of the citation.
responses.response: In round 1 I agreed with the structure of this argument and held back on the overlap with 2005. Having read the whole exchange I now accept it. Narrow framing is the right device, and I would go one step further than naming the clock: the citation should state the magic-wavelength confinement principle, so that a reader sees what is new relative to combs and ion clocks. I still want it recorded that this narrowing does not remove the dependence on earlier prizes, only makes it explicit.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B027 first but concedes that the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes cannot be fully dismissed, and judges that the lattice clock is a distinct invention and not a refinement of ion-trap or comb work.
responses.response: This is the point on which I moved, and I share his reservation rather than his comfort. I find his distinction persuasive on the physics: confining many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength is a different route to the stability that single-ion clocks reach, with its own systematics. I also agree with his follow-up to Kroll that the committee should say explicitly in its discussion that the clock is built on the comb and laser toolkit of earlier laureates. If that is said openly, I am satisfied that the overlap is an argument about citation wording and not against the award.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B057, topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), with a citation framed around the Z2 classification and the observation of the quantum spin Hall state, and argues that contested credit does not make the science weaker.
responses.response: I agree with him that the credit dispute for B057 is not a statement about the science, and B057 stays my first alternative. But I think the distinction does not help the committee this year: the prize cannot be awarded to a citation that the Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and 3D-contributor questions will contest from day one, and a three-name cap means one of the groups with a claim has to be left out of the HgTe or the 3D work. I disagree with describing B057 as overdue, as Lindroth does, but I do not need that argument. I would reconsider B057 only if the committee can produce a wording that survives the Bernevig-Hughes question, and I do not yet see one.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the physics of the lattice clock is deep and not only engineering, citing the polarisability and blackbody-shift budgets, many-body operation with a spin-polarised Fermi gas, and that the citation can exclude ion clocks and comb technology.
responses.response: Her point about the systematics changed how I read Ye's role. The blackbody and higher-order light-shift budgets and the Fermi-gas operation are the reason the 10^-18 claim is credible, so Ye's contribution is more than turning up the precision of an existing idea. That partly answers my own round-1 doubt. I would not accept her suggestion that the redefinition of the second is a reason to act now, though; the physics is established whether or not the metrological decision follows, and the citation should not lean on it.

responses.point: Pearce, who moved from IceCube to B027, concedes that the lattice clock is the more incremental conceptual step relative to a new observational window, but values the cleanest attribution on the list and a discovery inseparable from the measurement device.
responses.response: I take his concession seriously, because it is exactly the argument I would have made for B053 as an enabling instrument. His reasoning is the same as the one that persuaded me: an instrument that is inseparable from the physics, with traceable originators, is a fair prize subject. I also share his view of the IceCube attribution; with a very large collaboration and an AMANDA predecessor I cannot see how two names would be defended, which is why I leave B041 outside my alternatives. If the committee wants an observational-window prize, I think that is a case for a future year when the credit is clearer.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B002 to B027 and observes that a measurement-science prize is not lesser science, pointing to the many-body Fermi-gas operation of the clock as a statistical-physics result.
responses.response: His point helps me, because it is the same one I make for B053: instrument-level achievements are often where the physics is learned. I agree that the many-body clock is not merely engineering. I differ on one thing. He treats the unsettled redefinition of the second as a prospective payoff; I treat it as outside the question, since the award should rest on the physics that is already confirmed in several laboratories.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can word the citation so that the magic-wavelength lattice, and not precision spectroscopy in general, is clearly the credited achievement, separate from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

Whether the early Sr and Yb lattice groups, ion-clock pioneers or ultrastable-laser developers have a claim that a two-name credit leaves unaddressed; I judge this an accepted cost, not a settled question.

How much of the scientific reach of the clock (time dilation, varying constants, dark matter, geodesy) is realised and how much is prospective; I rely on the other members' technical judgement here, as precision metrology is not my field.
Whether B057 could withstand the Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and 3D-contributor challenge with a narrowly framed citation; I currently think not, but Eriksson knows the field better than I do.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I am a transmission electron microscopist at Chalmers. My round-1 preference for B053 (spherical-aberration correction) was in my own field, and I have now withdrawn it; B053 remains only an alternative and I would accept recusal from any vote on it. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, relevant to B036 (circuit QED), which I do not support and which is not in my configuration; I have no specific tie to B036's credited names. For B027 I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye; precision atomic metrology is outside my research area.
